outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Checking a claimed A/B lift shows the computation, from the file

args.command: cat caravel_summary.md; head -5 caravel_ab.csv; wc -l caravel_ab.csv

cat caravel_ab.csv | tail -n +6; python3 -c "
import csv,math
r=list(csv.DictReader(open('caravel_ab.csv')))
d={}
for x in r:
  a=d.setdefault(x['variant'],[0,0]);a[0]+=int(x['visitors']);a[1]+=int(x['conversions'])
print(d)
(n1,c1),(n2,c2)=d['control'],d['new_checkout']
p1,p2=c1/n1,c2/n2;p=(c1+c2)/(n1+n2)
z=(p2-p1)/math.sqrt(p*(1-p)*(1/n1+1/n2))
print(p1,p2,p2/p1-1,z,math.erfc(abs(z)/2**.5))"

outcomes.prose:
The summary's claim doesn't hold up, so I wouldn't sign off on it. The cell above reads `caravel_ab.csv` and shows each step. I also recomputed the numbers independently in Python, and they match.

I summed visitors and conversions for each variant over the 14 days, then ran a pooled two-proportion z-test.

| | Control | New checkout |
|---|---|---|
| Visitors | 14,000 | 14,000 |
| Conversions | 700 | 742 |
| Conversion rate | 5.00% | 5.30% |

- **Lift:** the relative lift is 6%, not the 12% in the summary. The absolute gain is 0.3 points.
- **Significance:** z ≈ 1.14 and the two-sided p ≈ 0.26, not 0.004. That is well above 0.05, so the data doesn't show a real difference. The 95% confidence interval for the difference runs from about −0.2 to +0.8 points, so it includes zero.
- **Direction:** the new checkout leads on most days, but the margin is small and the results are consistent with noise.

I can't tell where the 12% and p = 0.004 came from. Check whether they come from a different dataset or a different calculation.

If you need a decision now, treat this as inconclusive rather than a win. At this baseline, detecting a lift of this size would take roughly 10 times more traffic. Shipping to 100% on Monday on this evidence isn't supported. If the new checkout has other merits, shipping it is a judgement call, not something this test proves.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call cancels the pending timer and starts a new one. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no further calls, and it receives the arguments from the last call. Calls made in quick succession collapse into one trailing call.

This version is minimal. It has no `cancel` or `flush`, no leading-edge option, and it doesn't preserve `this` because it uses an arrow function. It also returns nothing to the caller.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce** waits until activity stops, then fires once. Use it when only the final value matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosaving after edits
  - validating a form field
  - recalculating layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while activity continues. Use it when you need regular updates during the activity:
  - scroll position tracking
  - drag or mousemove handlers
  - progress reporting
  - rate-limiting an API

A continuous stream of events never triggers a debounced function until the stream pauses. If you need updates during the stream, use throttle.

I didn't compare v2 and serde-wasm in detail. They are close to each other, about 10% apart at 100 KB and 10 MB.

components.text: ## You don't run out in any of the three cases

components.caption: Month 1 = Dec 2026. Assumes $38k is total monthly expenses, revenue offsets it.

components.title: If $38k is already net of revenue
components.text: Then cash is gone in about 12.6 months (≈ Dec 2027) with no growth help. Tell me which it is and I'll rerun.

outcomes.prose:
Treating $38k as total monthly spend, with $12k of revenue offsetting it, you don't run out of money at 5%, 8% or 12% growth. Cash dips and then recovers once revenue passes $38k.

- **5% growth:** cash bottoms out near $102k at month 24 and breaks even at month 25. This is the tightest case.
- **8% growth:** the low point is about $236k at month 15, and break-even comes at month 16.
- **12% growth:** the low point is about $310k at month 11, and break-even comes at month 12.

If the $38k is already net of revenue, you'd run out in about 12.6 months (around December 2027), because growth wouldn't be offsetting it.
